questions.prompt: You're running Drill 1 (The Cold Call) with your pod leader. What are the five pass criteria you must hit?
choices: Canonical opener from memory, upfront contract in first 60 seconds, three Investigate questions including 'what initially got you interested?', three-point price anchor, and close with 'are you opposed to getting set up today?'
Deliver the opener, close on price, and book a follow-up.
Follow the exact script word-for-word without improvisation.
Run through the nine product-knowledge data points verbally.
questions.explanation: Drill 1 pass criteria are exactly these five: canonical opener (from memory, no reading), upfront contract in first 60 seconds, at least three Investigate questions including the magic 'what initially got you interested?', three-point price anchor, and the magic close. Missing any one fails the drill.

questions.prompt: In Drill 2 (Objection Circle), your pod leader tells you: 'You failed.' You think you did fine. She says 'You said I totally understand three times.' Why is that an auto-fail?
choices: It's grammatically redundant.
'I totally understand' is banned — the drill's explicit pass criteria include 'no I totally understand' because it sounds scripted and breaks the 'sincere one-word ack plus question' pattern.
It eats up too much time.
The pod leader just doesn't like that phrase.
questions.explanation: Drill 2 pass criteria explicitly include 'no I totally understand.' The phrase signals trained delivery and puts the lead on guard. The approved replacement is a sincere one-word ack ('Gotcha') then a question. This isn't preference — it's a measured close-rate issue.

questions.prompt: Your pod leader assigns you The Bodybuilder on Recovery as your Drill 3 archetype. What's his canonical profile, and what's the right tier move?
choices: Big guy, lifts heavy, curious about Pilates for recovery only — wants to discount the unlimited and buy 4-session only. The right move is to meet him on 4-session, not force the unlimited.
Emotionally loaded lead who needs empathy plus a firm close.
Hostile and pushy — requires a professional takeaway.
Competitor defector who needs the hive-mind social proof.
questions.explanation: The Bodybuilder on Recovery is explicitly described: big guy, lifts heavy, Pilates for recovery only, wants to discount unlimited and buy 4-session. Forcing unlimited mismatches the investigation; matching his stated use case (4-session as recovery tool) is the appropriate tier move.

questions.prompt: Drill 4 (Self-Listen Review) asks you to pull three of your own calls. What mix and what must you demonstrate?
choices: Three wins; demonstrate your best pitch.
Two losses and one win; articulate which DRIVE step you executed well, which you skipped or rushed, and one specific thing you'll do differently next call — without your pod leader telling you.
Three random calls; your pod leader diagnoses.
Three losses; demonstrate emotional resilience.
questions.explanation: Drill 4 is explicitly two losses + one win. Pass criteria: you can articulate your own gaps without your pod leader telling you. This is the primary feedback loop for pitch improvement — self-diagnosis is the skill being tested, not call-selection or resilience.

questions.prompt: A new brand gets added to your pod mid-engagement. What does the brand-specific certification compress to, and what's the first-day production expectation?
choices: Full Phase 1 + Phase 2 all over again at full duration.
No certification required — jump straight to calls.
The brand-specific cert compresses to a 30-minute session and first-day production expectation is halved.
A full day of shadowing before any live calls.
questions.explanation: Mid-engagement brand additions compress brand-specific cert to a 30-minute session, with first-day production halved. The generic cert doesn't repeat because it's brand-agnostic; the halved expectation exists so reps can ramp without burning leads.

questions.prompt: Your manager plays back your call and says 'What's their why?' What is she diagnosing?
choices: You skipped the opener.
Your three-point price anchor was in the wrong order.
You forgot to use the utility text 'how do you want to proceed?'
You didn't investigate deeply enough — the why-chain didn't reach the emotional motivation under the stated goal.
questions.explanation: The coaching shorthand 'What's their why?' is a diagnosis for shallow Investigate — you stopped at the stated goal instead of chasing the emotional weight underneath. That emotional weight is closing ammunition; without it the pitch feels generic and the close stalls.

questions.prompt: Your manager says 'Reserve the close' during a call review. What specific mistake is she pointing to?
choices: You didn't close hard enough at the end.
You skipped the upfront contract — the 'if we both agree this is a fit, I can save you more on our founding memberships. Is that fair?' move before the pitch started.
You double-booked the lead.
You forgot to ask for a referral.
questions.explanation: 'Reserve the close' = 'you skipped the upfront contract.' The R step in DRIVE pre-authorizes the price discussion and harvests the first yes of the call — skipping it is the single most common reason calls stall at pricing. The phrase is a diagnosis, not a close-style comment.

questions.prompt: A new rep says 'I hate listening to my own calls — it's embarrassing.' What's the growth-mindset response from the module?
choices: Embarrassing yourself IS the learning mechanism. First call is awkward, tenth is less, hundredth is automatic. Listen to your worst calls — that's where the next improvement lives.
She's right — self-review isn't for everyone. Skip it.
Only listen to your wins so you don't lose confidence.
Have a pod leader listen for you and report back.
questions.explanation: The growth-mindset section is explicit: embarrassing yourself is the learning mechanism. The discomfort is where the improvement comes from. Skipping self-review or listening only to wins kills the primary feedback loop; outsourcing the review defeats the point — she needs to hear herself.

questions.prompt: On the final north star: 'Sales is communication. You're not pushing, you're ___.' Fill in the canonical word.
choices: persuading.
closing.
matching — matching their stated goals to our offer, their emotional weight to our value proposition, their price comfort to our tier structure. If the match is real, the sale closes itself.
convincing.
questions.explanation: The final north star reframes the job as matching, not pushing. Match stated goals to offer, emotional weight to value prop, price comfort to tier. The match-based frame is why the DRIVE emphasizes Investigate so hard — if you don't find the match, there's nothing to close on.

questions.prompt: The weekly practice rhythm after certification has four components. Which of these is NOT one of them?
choices: Friday 1-1 with pod leader: half pitch practice, half objection circle.
Weekly objection circle (group, 15 min), one objection per rep, rotate.
Monthly call review (team, 30 min): one rep brings a recorded call they lost, team diagnoses together.
Daily full-team roleplay session (60 min) where every rep runs DRIVE in front of everyone.
questions.explanation: The four canonical rhythm components are Friday 1-1, weekly group objection circle, monthly team call review, and ongoing self-review (three own calls per week). Daily team roleplay isn't in the module — the weekly/monthly cadence is calibrated so reps have time to actually sell.
